auraIntro: Explorer, Andromeda briefing loaded. Review the metrics for our nearest major galactic neighbor.
overview: The Andromeda Galaxy (Messier 31) is a giant spiral galaxy located approximately 2.5 million light-years from Earth. It is the largest member of our Local Group.
formation: Assembled through galactic collisions approximately 10 billion years ago.
structure: Classic spiral galaxy with a double stellar nucleus containing a supermassive black hole.
discoveryHistory: Cataloged by Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi in 964 CE as a 'small cloud'. Edwin Hubble proved its extragalactic nature in 1923.
observationTips: Visible to the naked eye under dark skies as a hazy patch; impressive through binoculars.
funFacts: Andromeda contains approximately 1 trillion stars—more than twice as many as the Milky Way.
It is traveling toward our galaxy at 110 kilometers per second.

cards.title: Arrival: Colossus of the Local Group
cards.subtitle: Messier 31 Overview
cards.body: Spanning over 220,000 light-years across space, Andromeda (M31) is the giant anchor of our Local Group. Located 2.5 million light-years away, this magnificent spiral galaxy contains an estimated 1 trillion stars and is surrounded by satellite dwarf galaxies like M32 and M110.

cards.title: Discovery: Proving the Extragalactic Scale
cards.subtitle: From Persian Astronomy to Edwin Hubble
cards.body: First recorded by Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi in 964 CE as a 'little cloud', Andromeda's true nature remained mysterious for centuries. In 1923, Edwin Hubble identified Cepheid variable stars in M31, proving conclusively that it lay far outside the Milky Way and settling the Great Debate on the scale of the cosmos.
bulletPoints: Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi documented M31 in his Book of Fixed Stars in 964 CE.
Charles Messier cataloged it as M31 in 1764.
Edwin Hubble's 1923 Cepheid measurement proved M31 was an independent galaxy.

visualPlaceholder.title: Hubble 1923 VAR Glass Plate
visualPlaceholder.caption: Historical photographic plate where Edwin Hubble wrote 'VAR!' discovering Cepheid variables in M31.

cards.title: Cosmic Story: Double Nucleus & Gravitational Core
cards.subtitle: P1 and P2 Core Structure
cards.body: Hubble observations revealed that Andromeda possesses a double optical nucleus (P1 and P2) at its core. This unique appearance is caused by an eccentric ring of aging blue stars orbiting a central supermassive black hole containing roughly 100 million solar masses.
bulletPoints: P1 and P2 optical peaks represent stars at the apastron of an elliptical disk orbit.
Surrounded by over 460 globular clusters, including massive Mayall II (G1).
Tidal interactions with companion galaxies M32 and M110 warp its outer gas disk.

visualPlaceholder.caption: High-resolution view of Andromeda's central core showing the P1/P2 optical nucleus.

cards.title: Deep Insight: Resolving 200 Million Stars
cards.subtitle: Hubble's Monumental 2025 Panoramic Survey
cards.body: In 2025, NASA released an expanded Hubble panorama of Andromeda combining over 600 overlapping snapshots taken across a decade. This monumental image resolves approximately 200 million individual stars in the galaxy's disk, allowing scientists to analyze stellar evolution across entire galactic neighborhoods.
bulletPoints: Combined 600+ Hubble fields of view to map 200 million stars.
Traces star formation history across 100,000 light-years of disk area.
Enormous outer gas halo extends halfway across space to the Milky Way.

visualPlaceholder.title: Hubble Panoramic Survey of M31
visualPlaceholder.caption: Hubble Space Telescope high-definition stellar panorama resolving millions of individual stars in M31.

cards.title: Cosmic Curiosity: The Inevitable Merger
cards.subtitle: 110 km/s Approach Velocity
cards.body: Andromeda and the Milky Way are approaching each other at 110 kilometers per second. In approximately 4.5 billion years, both colossal spiral systems will collide head-on, creating dramatic tidal tails of gas before settling into a combined giant elliptical galaxy.
bulletPoints: Approaching speed equals ~400,000 km/h toward the Milky Way.
Gravitational tides will distort both galaxies into glowing streams.
Future observers on Earth would see Andromeda fill the entire night sky before collision.
